messages.author: 156a0be20e5567ba
messages.subject: Resuming stoped chains
parts:
Hi,

I am running Stan on a cluster computer with a hard wall-time limit. However, the chains I run sometimes take longer than this limit. Is there a way to tell stan to dump the state of its RNG every now and then, and then to resume a chain from a given state?

Thanks!
Heiko

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Resuming stoped chains
parts:
Currently no. Although I think there was some (unmerged) progress made on resuming a sampler after completing an initial run, I doubt it would work reliably if the server SIGTERMs the process.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Resuming stoped chains
parts:
Being able to dump

* PRNG state

* adaptation state (mass matrix, time discretization [i.e., step size])

* parameter state

No fundamental problem, but the PRNG state is a bit tricky given
the kind of PRNG we use, and we have to be careful to round trip any
floating point through I/O reliably (binary or lots of digits printed).

It's still not clear to me restarting from where the sampler left off
is ever a good idea, because you usually want to go back and do more
adaptation and then restart sampling from a better adaptation state.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Resuming stoped chains
parts:
That's a motivation I hadn't thought about.

Restarting adaptation is a bit trickier because we're
using online estimators for the mass matrix. To properly
restart from exactly where we left off, those would need
to be dumped too, which is exposing a lot more of our internals
to the outside than I'm comfortable with. So maybe we could
compromise and just store mass matrix and step size at some
point and put a little more burden on the caller to rewind
and restart from the last saved state. But that could lose
days in a 6 day run.

By the way, what's taking 6 days to run?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Resuming stoped chains
parts:
Do you really need full Bayes for that? Are you doing
downstream inference with the parameter estimation uncertainty?

If not, are the posterior means or medians that different
different than what you'd get with a penalized MLE?

This is exactly the kind of problem for which we want to expand
our MLE capabilities to use Laplace approximations of uncertainty.
Not to mention apply MML, VB, or EP for hierarchical models. Sorry
we're not there yet!

- Bob

messages.author: 146bc26797d1c5e2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Resuming stoped chains
parts:
Sorry if this is obvious, maybe it isn't for all who want to do logistic regression with Stan:

If there's no hierarchy, that is if priors are fixed,  and priors are differentiable (not like Lasso/L1), one can take the MAP estimate with Stan's optimizing(). The default LBFGS is fine,  and let it compute the Hessian (I haven't tried that). Then 1.96*sqrt(diag(solve(-hessian))) gives you the 95% confidence intervals based on the first-order Laplace approximation. (Or is it called second order because the first derivative vanishes?)

If you are not using R, "solve" above is the inverse. 

Joint MAP of all parameters is not so good for estimating hierarchies, or "automatic shrinkage". So there a strategy for large data is to use the Laplace approximation internally in the optimization algorithm, something the current Stan cannot do.

On Wednesday, November 12, 2014 5:39:28 PM UTC+2, Allen Riddell wrote:
I see. Yes, Laplace approx would be fine in this case. It would be great if Stan
could do that for us!

When I tryed to work on resume sampling, the PRNG was the least of the
problems, I was able to save it using just streams and << operators like
in the example bellow:

#include <iostream>
#include <sstream>
#include <fstream>
#include <string>
#include "boost/random.hpp"
#include "boost/generator_iterator.hpp"

int main(int /*argc*/, char** /*argv*/)
{
boost::ecuyer1988 rng1;
boost::ecuyer1988 rng2;

rng1(); rng1(); rng1();

std::string state;
{
std::ifstream myfile;
myfile.open ("example.txt");
myfile >> rng2;
myfile.close();
}

std::cout << "state: " << state << std::endl;
std::cout << "rngs state comparison: " << (rng1 == rng2) << std::endl;

parts: Indeed, Marcus is working on automating all these things within Stan.
On Nov 12, 2014, at 1:44 PM, Janne Sinkkonen <janne.s...@gmail.com> wrote:

Sorry if this is obvious, maybe it isn't for all who want to do logistic regression with Stan:

If there's no hierarchy, that is if priors are fixed,  and priors are differentiable (not like Lasso/L1), one can take the MAP estimate with Stan's optimizing(). The default LBFGS is fine,  and let it compute the Hessian (I haven't tried that). Then 1.96*sqrt(diag(solve(-hessian))) gives you the 95% confidence intervals based on the first-order Laplace approximation. (Or is it called second order because the first derivative vanishes?)

If you are not using R, "solve" above is the inverse. 

Joint MAP of all parameters is not so good for estimating hierarchies, or "automatic shrinkage". So there a strategy for large data is to use the Laplace approximation internally in the optimization algorithm, something the current Stan cannot do.

On Wednesday, November 12, 2014 5:39:28 PM UTC+2, Allen Riddell wrote:
I see. Yes, Laplace approx would be fine in this case. It would be great if Stan
could do that for us!

requires a bit more work if we wind up needing to save during
warmup because there's dynamic state with the mass matrix
estimates which work online using Welford's algorithm.

as high priority to-do items:

for hierarchical models along the lines of lme4 (but with different
algorithms that we are hoping will generlize beyond hierarchical
glms.

a bit trickier and may not get done right away)
